title: Motor Overcurrent
description: Diagnose high motor current causing overload trips

n1.text: Motor's pulling too much current. Let's figure out why. First — can you see the conveyor belt? Is there anything jammed or piled up on it?
n1.hint: Look along the full length of the belt, especially at transfer points and under guards.

options.label: Yes, there's a jam
options.transition: There's your problem. A jam makes the motor work way harder than it should.

options.label: No, belt looks clear
options.transition: OK, belt's clear. Let's check the mechanical side.

n2.text: Put your hand near the motor housing (don't touch if it's hot). Can you feel excessive heat? And listen — any grinding or unusual noise from the bearings?
n2.hint: A healthy motor hums evenly. Grinding, squealing, or rattling means bearing trouble.

options.label: Yes, hot and/or noisy
options.transition: That points to bearing failure. The motor is fighting itself.

options.label: No, seems normal
options.transition: Good, motor itself seems OK mechanically. Let's look at the load.

n3.text: Check the belt tension — push down on the belt between pulleys. Does it deflect more than about half an inch, or does it feel really tight?
n3.hint: Too tight = extra load on the motor. Too loose = slipping, which also increases current.

options.label: Too tight
options.transition: That'll do it. Over-tensioned belt puts a constant extra load on the motor.

options.label: Too loose
options.transition: A slipping belt makes the motor work harder trying to maintain speed.

options.label: Feels about right
options.transition: Tension's fine. Let's look at the actual current reading.

n4.text: Let's get a current reading. If you've got a clamp meter, measure the motor current on one of the supply leads. What's the reading compared to the nameplate FLA?
n4.hint: Nameplate Full Load Amps is on the motor data plate. Current should be at or below FLA under normal load.

options.label: Way over FLA (>120%)
options.transition: That's significantly over nameplate. Something is loading this motor beyond its rating.

options.label: Near FLA or slightly over
options.transition: It's borderline. Could be a sizing issue or gradually increasing load.

options.label: Can't measure right now
options.transition: No worries, let's check a couple more things.

n5.text: One more thing — is this a VFD-driven motor? Check if there are any fault codes on the VFD display.
n5.hint: VFD faults like 'OC' (overcurrent) or 'OL' (overload) would confirm the issue. The VFD may also show real-time current.

options.label: Yes, VFD shows fault
options.transition: The VFD caught it. Let's see what it's telling us.

options.label: No VFD, or no fault shown
options.transition: Alright, let's address the overcurrent directly.

n_jam.text: Clear the jam and the current should come right back down. But don't just pull stuff out while it's running.
steps: Stop the conveyor (use the normal stop, not E-stop unless it's urgent)
Lock out and tag out before reaching into the conveyor
Clear the jammed material
Inspect the belt and rollers for damage from the jam
Reset the overload relay if it tripped
Restart and verify current is back to normal

n_bearings.text: Bearing failure is causing the overcurrent. The motor needs to come offline before it burns up.
steps: Stop the motor immediately
Lock out and tag out the motor disconnect
Check if the shaft can be rotated by hand — if it's seized, the bearings are gone
Schedule motor bearing replacement or full motor swap
Check coupling alignment when reinstalling

n_tension.text: Belt tension is off, which is making the motor draw extra current. Good news — this is an easy fix.
steps: Stop the conveyor
Adjust the take-up to get proper belt tension (check the manual for spec)
Typical deflection is 1/2" to 3/4" between pulleys
Restart and verify motor current drops back to normal range

n_overloaded.text: The motor is being overloaded beyond its capacity. This could be a process issue or a motor sizing issue.
steps: Reduce the load on the conveyor if possible
Check if product weight or throughput has increased recently
Verify the motor HP matches the application requirement
If the overload keeps tripping, don't just bump up the OL setting — find the root cause
Consider upsizing the motor if the process legitimately needs more capacity

n_vfd.text: The VFD is faulting on overcurrent. Let's clear it and address the root cause.
steps: Record the VFD fault code before clearing
Check VFD parameters: acceleration time may be too fast (increase accel ramp)
Verify motor nameplate data matches VFD motor setup parameters
Clear the fault and restart
If it faults again immediately, the load is genuinely too high for the motor
